FaultFinder
ML Ratchet · BuildingSim phase 2

FaultFinder

Give it one day of an air handler's trend log. It says how likely the unit is faulty and which fault it looks like. It never saw a real fault while learning: every training example came from a simulated building.

Trained on physics. Graded on reality: 217 real lab and building days.

Real exam days

Pick a day, read the log, compare the verdicts

Every exam day is here: Iowa's twin air handlers (one faulted, one healthy on the same day), LBNL's FLEXLAB test cell, Oak Ridge's rooftop unit and Nesbitt Hall, an occupied university building in Philadelphia. None of them was used to train or choose anything. The rule baseline and FaultFinder are scored on the same day. Drag across the chart to read the sensors on the schematic above.

The ratchet

Each rung had to beat the last one

How it was built

Physics, real noise, then a small network

1 · Simulator

BuildingSim, the collection's building simulator: a 5R1C zone heat balance with sun, wind-driven infiltration, moisture, and air handlers built from fan laws, mixing boxes, coils, chillers, boilers and DX curves from DOE reference data. Its checks: RC step response within 0.003 K of the closed form, 31 of 36 BESTEST results inside the reference range, psychrometrics within 0.02 K of CoolProp, and 26 of 26 fault signatures moving in the expected direction.

2 · Fault bank

Two banks of 39,000 simulated days each (the final model trains on the calibrated one): random offices, schools, shops and hotels with rooftop units or VAV air handlers, in 17 US climates, any season. Each 12-day window runs twice, healthy and with one of 20 BuildingSim fault types from day 5 on (stuck or leaking dampers and valves, fouled coils, refrigerant charge, low airflow, sensor offsets, economizer and schedule faults, VAV box stuck). These map to 18 FaultFinder classes.

3 · Real noise

Sensor noise and hunting are copied from real fault-free dev days (residual library), plus static sensor disagreements, sensor drift when the fan stops, logger gaps and each exam source's set of logged points. The 20 Korean office AHUs (unlabelled) set the start/stop irregularity and the tail of supply-air tracking error.

4 · Twin tests on dev

Simulating each dev day's twin found two mismatches. Building automation logs commands: a heating valve stuck open logs 0 % while BuildingSim logs the true 100 %. And a real damper at 100 % command lets in only 81–90 % outdoor air, while the simulator's damper signal is the outdoor-air fraction itself. Both became rungs.

5 · Network

A 1-D convolutional network over one local day (96 × 15 min, 35 feature rows: temperatures, physical differences such as mixed minus return, estimated outdoor-air fraction, actuators, fan power, time of day and which channels exist). 161k weights. Outputs: P(fault), a softmax over 18 fault classes, a severity and the day's extra HVAC energy.

6 · Calibration and exam

The 20 dev unit-days (seven at Iowa, three FLEXLAB, two ORNL, eight Nesbitt) were the only real data used for anything: the noise library, the twin tests, the dev gate and the temperature. The 217 exam days were run once, with the final model, after the ladder was closed.

Where it fails

Limits

  • Diagnosis barely beats a guess. Top-1 accuracy on real faulty days is about the same as always naming the most common fault. Use the top three as a list of things to check, not as an answer.
  • Too many false alarms at the default threshold. About a third of healthy days get P(fault) above 0.5. Real units run in ways the simulator never does (Nesbitt's air handler runs all night with the chiller off; zone and return sensors disagree by 1.5 K at Oak Ridge). For alarms, use a stricter threshold and accept fewer catches.
  • Probabilities are squashed toward 0.5. One temperature fitted on 20 days over-corrected; the ranking (AUC) is unaffected.
  • Rooftop units: worse than a one-line rule on 17 ORNL days (AUC 0.65 vs 0.72). Its faults (condenser fouling, infiltration, lighting schedule, zone sensor) leave little trace in the few points an RTU logs.
  • One day at a time, one zone. It does not compare a day with the unit's own history, and BuildingSim has one zone, ideal controls, no exhaust damper, return fan or duct leak. Those faults are only caught when they disturb something else.
  • Small exam. 217 days from five facilities; the 90 % interval on AHU AUC is about ±0.06.
Use it

The release

faultfinder-v1.0.zip holds a numpy-only model (101k weights), a reader for trend logs with the column names below, a demo on four real exam days, the model card and every training script.

pip install numpy pandas
python demo.py                       # four real exam days, a few seconds
python pipeline.py my_ahu_day.csv    # columns: time_local, T_oa T_ra T_ma T_sa T_sa_sp T_zone,
                                     # damper_oa valve_cc valve_hc fan_sa_speed fan_sa_power_kW fan_sa_status occ
                                     # (degC, 0..1, kW, 0/1); any subset, missing channels are allowed

Part of ML Ratchet (github.com/dogum/ML-Ratchet). FaultFinder is a research model: it flags days for a person to look at, it does not replace commissioning.
